title: Sass/SCSS: Modules, Mixins, and Maintainable CSS
description: Use Sass features deliberately, understand what compiles to CSS, and choose between Sass variables and runtime CSS custom properties.
learningOutcomes: Explain Sass compilation and its boundaries.
Use Sass modules, variables, maps and mixins deliberately.
Compare compile-time Sass variables with runtime CSS custom properties.
Debug the emitted CSS and avoid deep nesting.

blocks.text: What Sass adds—and what remains CSS

SCSS is a stylesheet syntax that compiles into CSS. It adds variables, module imports, mixins, functions, maps and controlled generation, but it does not replace the browser's CSS cascade or layout engine. Sass variables are resolved during compilation; CSS custom properties remain in the browser and can change at runtime or under a theme selector. Choose the feature whose lifecycle matches the job.

steps.title: Load modules before ordinary rules
steps.explanation: @use belongs before ordinary style rules. Namespaces make the origin of map.get and color.scale explicit.

steps.title: Define compile-time values
steps.explanation: The map groups named values, but it is not sent to the browser as a Sass map.

steps.title: Check generated selectors and color output
steps.explanation: The browser receives ordinary CSS. color.scale is namespaced and avoids the deprecated global darken() call used in old examples.

items: Use partial files such as _tokens.scss and load them through @use with a namespace; @forward can build a deliberate public module API.
Mixins are useful for repeated declaration patterns with arguments. If you only need a set of values, variables/maps are usually simpler.
Functions should calculate and return values; avoid hiding large amounts of unrelated emitted CSS inside abstractions.
The legacy interactive source uses @import examples. Sass deprecated Sass @import in Dart Sass 1.80.0; follow current module-system guidance rather than copying that old pattern unchanged.
Use CSS custom properties for runtime theming or values that must be changed by selectors/JavaScript after the stylesheet is loaded; use Sass variables for compile-time organization.

blocks.title: Debug the generated CSS too
blocks.text: Browser DevTools shows the CSS the browser actually receives, not the SCSS source abstraction. When a nested rule or mixin surprises you, inspect compiled output, the selector that matched, source order and specificity before adding more nesting.

blocks.prompt: When should a CSS custom property usually be preferred over a Sass variable?

options.text: When the value must change at runtime under a theme or selector
options.feedback: CSS custom properties remain in the browser and participate in the cascade, so a theme can override them at runtime.

options.text: Whenever the value is used more than once, regardless of lifecycle
options.feedback: Re-use matters, but the runtime-versus-compile-time distinction determines the most suitable mechanism.

options.text: When the browser needs to execute Sass syntax directly
options.feedback: Browsers do not execute SCSS; it must be compiled to CSS.
CSS custom properties are a CSS feature and are not tied to a particular framework.

blocks.explanation: Think about when and where the value needs to change, not just whether it is reusable.

blocks.title: Refactor repeated styles into a small Sass module
blocks.context: Convert duplicated styles into an intentional token/module structure and inspect the CSS it emits.
instructions: Create a _tokens.scss module with named spacing and color values.
Load the module using @use rather than a legacy @import.
Use a mixin only for a repeated declaration pattern that benefits from parameters.
Replace deep nesting with shallow selectors and explain the resulting specificity.
Create a CSS custom property for a value that must change between light/dark theme at runtime.
requirements: Module dependencies are explicit and namespaced.
Generated CSS contains the intended selectors and values.
Nesting does not generate accidental high-specificity selectors.
Compile-time Sass variables and runtime CSS custom properties are used intentionally.
The solution follows modern Sass module guidance.
hints: @use creates a namespace; use the namespace when accessing an exported variable.
Use shallow nesting and inspect the compiled selector.
A CSS variable such as --color-surface can be overridden by a theme selector at runtime.
successCriteria: Shared tokens live in a namespaced Sass module.
A compiled CSS result is checked against intent.
Runtime and compile-time values are distinguished.

blocks.text: A Sass @use belongs at the top of the stylesheet, before ordinary rules and declarations. It loads a module once and exposes members through a namespace, so a reader can see where map.get or color.scale comes from. Sass variables are resolved while compiling; the browser receives CSS, not the Sass map, loop or mixin. If compilation fails, inspect the Sass build output first; if the rule compiles but loses in the page, switch to browser DevTools and investigate cascade, specificity and source order.

steps.title: Pass an intentional parameter to a mixin
steps.explanation: This mixin emits a focus-visible outline where it is included. It can be useful when several controls need the same declaration pattern with a chosen color; a one-off declaration may be simpler than introducing the mixin.

steps.title: A loop emits one selector per map entry
steps.explanation: The map holds build-time names and values. The compiler emits .gap-sm and .gap-md rules; adding map values increases output CSS, so generate only utilities the design system actually needs.

steps.title: Inspect both source and emitted CSS
steps.explanation: @include expands the mixin's declarations into the button rule. DevTools shows the compiled selector and computed focus style, not the original Sass abstraction.

blocks.prompt: Given the map `(sm: 0.5rem, md: 1rem)`, what does the @each loop in the walkthrough emit?

options.text: One CSS custom property that changes when the user selects a theme
options.feedback: The map and loop are evaluated at build time; they do not create a browser-controlled theme value.

options.text: Two CSS rules, .gap-sm and .gap-md, with their corresponding gap values
options.feedback: The loop iterates over the two map entries and interpolation places each key in a selector.

options.text: A runtime JavaScript loop executed for every rendered element
options.feedback: Sass runs during compilation, not in the browser's JavaScript runtime.

options.text: A single .gap-* selector with a variable value
options.feedback: Interpolation generates concrete selector names; ordinary CSS does not receive the Sass loop variable.

blocks.explanation: Sass generation turns compile-time data into ordinary CSS. Keep generated selector families bounded and purposeful.

blocks.text: Choose mixins and @extend by their output behavior

A mixin copies declarations into each place that includes it and can accept arguments; this makes the call site explicit but can repeat output. @extend changes selector relationships so selectors share a rule; it may create broader or surprising selector combinations. A placeholder selector (%name) is omitted unless extended, but it still participates in selector unification. Prefer a mixin for parameterized behavior or explicit local output. Use @extend only when the selectors are truly substitutable and inspect the compiled CSS.

steps.title: A placeholder emits no standalone selector
steps.explanation: The compiled output groups the .notice selector with rules extended from %surface; the placeholder itself is not emitted as a class. Other selectors that extend it may join the selector list.

steps.title: A mixin emits declarations at the include site
steps.explanation: The parameter makes the background explicit at each call site. The declarations are repeated for .alert rather than joining a shared selector list; inspect output size and selector behavior for the real project.

blocks.title: Do not copy old global Sass APIs unreviewed
blocks.text: Dart Sass deprecated Sass @import and global built-in functions such as darken() and adjust-hue() in 1.80.0. Use the module system (for example @use 'sass:color' and color.scale()) for current examples. The old Notion snippets show historical syntax; their concepts remain useful, but the exact API should be modernized. Do not silence a warning before identifying whether it is generated by your code or a dependency.

blocks.prompt: Why should @use 'sass:map' and @use 'sass:color' be placed before the stylesheet's ordinary rules?

options.text: Sass modules are compile-time dependencies and @use must appear before ordinary stylesheet rules
options.feedback: The module system makes dependencies explicit and namespaced; place @use near the beginning of the stylesheet.

options.text: The browser must download the Sass modules at runtime
options.feedback: Sass compiles modules into CSS before the browser loads the page.

options.text: @use converts Sass variables into CSS custom properties automatically
options.feedback: Sass variables are compile-time values; runtime custom properties must be declared as CSS properties.

options.text: @use is only required when importing a CSS file from another domain
options.feedback: @use is Sass's module loading rule, not a browser cross-origin import.

blocks.explanation: Explicit module loading keeps member ownership visible and avoids the global namespace model of deprecated Sass @import.

blocks.title: Generate a small Sass utility set and inspect its CSS
blocks.context: A team has repeated spacing rules and inconsistent keyboard focus styles. Refactor only the values that belong in a build-time map and produce a shared, visible focus pattern.
instructions: Create a namespaced Sass module for spacing and load it with @use; keep @use at the top of the entry stylesheet.
Use a small map and @each loop to generate only the three spacing utility classes requested by the design system.
Write a focus-visible mixin with a clear parameter and include it in two controls.
Use color.scale or another namespaced sass:color function instead of an old global color function.
Compile the stylesheet and compare the generated CSS with the intended selectors; then inspect focus and cascade behavior in browser DevTools.
requirements: The module uses @use and the namespace is visible at each member access.
The generated utility set contains exactly the requested selectors, with no accidental unbounded selector generation.
Both controls expose a visible keyboard focus indicator.
The compiled CSS and any trade-off from repeated mixin declarations are described.
hints: Remember that @use creates a namespace; access the map through that namespace.
The each loop should emit three known classes because the map has exactly three entries.
Use :focus-visible so keyboard focus is apparent without assuming that every pointer interaction needs the same ring.
successCriteria: The build compiles with no Sass deprecation warning caused by this new code.
Exactly three spacing classes are emitted and their values match the source map.
Both controls have a visible, non-clipped keyboard focus indicator.
The learner explains that Sass variables and loops disappear into compiled CSS while CSS custom properties remain available at runtime.

items: Sass compiles authoring conveniences into ordinary CSS; the browser still applies the CSS cascade.
Prefer @use/@forward for explicit module boundaries; do not copy legacy @import examples without review.
Use Sass variables for build-time values and CSS custom properties for runtime theming.
